mediaWork.title: Junk Science and the American Criminal Justice System
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Forensic science misconduct, pseudoscience in courtrooms, wrongful convictions
mediaWork.summaryNotes:
"Junk Science and the American Criminal Justice System" examines how unreliable and unvalidated forensic techniques have been used to convict innocent people. The book focuses particularly on bite mark analysis, a now-discredited forensic technique that has contributed to numerous wrongful convictions. Fabricant provides an insider's view of the fight to overturn these convictions and to reform the use of forensic science in the American criminal justice system.

The book details specific cases where junk science led to wrongful convictions, the legal battles to overturn these convictions, and the broader efforts to reform forensic science practices in the United States. It also explores the racial disparities in how these flawed techniques have been applied, with a disproportionate impact on people of color.

mediaWork.title: Solitary: A Biography
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Wrongful conviction, solitary confinement, prison reform, racial justice
mediaWork.summaryNotes:
"Solitary" is Albert Woodfox's powerful memoir detailing his experience of being wrongfully convicted of murder and subsequently spending nearly 44 years in solitary confinement at Louisiana's notorious Angola Prison. The book chronicles Woodfox's early life, his political awakening as a member of the Black Panther Party, and his tireless fight for justice while enduring the psychological torture of extreme isolation.

Woodfox, along with Herman Wallace and Robert King (collectively known as the "Angola Three"), was convicted of the 1972 murder of a prison guard based on flimsy evidence and false testimony. The book details how their political activism as Black Panthers made them targets within the prison system, leading to their wrongful convictions and extreme punishment.

Throughout the memoir, Woodfox describes how he maintained his sanity and dignity during decades of solitary confinement, educating himself, organizing fellow prisoners, and never giving up hope for exoneration. His story is not only a personal account of survival but also a damning indictment of the American criminal justice system, particularly its treatment of Black men and its use of solitary confinement as punishment.

mediaWork.title: Blind Injustice: A Former Prosecutor Exposes the Psychology and Politics of Wrongful Convictions
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Psychological factors contributing to wrongful convictions, cognitive biases in the justice system
mediaWork.summaryNotes:
"Blind Injustice" examines the psychological and institutional factors that contribute to wrongful convictions. Drawing on his unique perspective as both a former prosecutor and later an innocence advocate, Mark Godsey explores how cognitive biases, institutional pressures, and psychological phenomena lead well-intentioned professionals in the criminal justice system to convict innocent people.

The book identifies several psychological factors that contribute to wrongful convictions, including tunnel vision, confirmation bias, memory malleability, administrative evil, and dehumanization. Godsey argues that these psychological factors affect all human beings, including judges, police officers, prosecutors, and jurors, making the system vulnerable to error despite good intentions.

Through case studies from his work with the Ohio Innocence Project and his own experiences as a prosecutor, Godsey illustrates how these psychological factors play out in real cases. He also proposes reforms to address these issues and reduce the likelihood of wrongful convictions.

mediaWork.title: Barred: Why the Innocent Can't Get Out of Prison
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Legal barriers to exoneration, procedural obstacles in post-conviction relief
mediaWork.summaryNotes:
"Barred" examines the procedural and institutional barriers that prevent innocent people from being exonerated after they have been wrongfully convicted. Medwed argues that the American criminal justice system is structured to prioritize finality over accuracy, making it extraordinarily difficult for wrongfully convicted individuals to overturn their convictions even when compelling evidence of their innocence emerges.

The book walks readers through the various procedural hurdles that wrongfully convicted people face at each stage of the post-conviction process, including strict filing deadlines, restrictive standards of review, limited access to evidence, and deference to lower court decisions. Medwed demonstrates how these procedural rules, which were designed to promote efficiency and finality, often function as insurmountable barriers for innocent people seeking justice.

Through case studies and legal analysis, Medwed reveals how the system's emphasis on procedural rules over substantive justice creates a situation where courts may acknowledge a person's likely innocence but still deny relief due to procedural technicalities. The book makes a compelling case for reform of the post-conviction process to better balance the interests of finality with the imperative to correct wrongful convictions.

mediaWork.title: That Bird Has My Wings: The Autobiography of an Innocent Man on Death Row
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Memoir, wrongful conviction, Buddhism, personal transformation
mediaWork.summaryNotes:
"That Bird Has My Wings" is Jarvis Jay Masters' memoir chronicling his difficult childhood, his path to incarceration, and his spiritual transformation while on death row at San Quentin. The book begins with Masters' early years, marked by poverty, foster care, abuse, and neglect after his mother's drug addiction led to the separation of their family. He recounts his experiences in various foster homes and juvenile detention facilities, where he experienced further abuse and began a path toward criminal behavior.

The memoir details Masters' eventual incarceration at San Quentin for armed robbery at age 19, and his subsequent conviction for participating in the 1985 murder of a prison guard, Sergeant Howell Burchfield—a crime for which he maintains his innocence. Masters describes how he was in his cell at the time of the murder but was implicated and sentenced to death.

The book also explores Masters' spiritual journey and his embrace of Buddhism while in prison, which helped him find meaning and purpose despite his circumstances. Through his practice and writing, Masters transformed his life within the confines of death row, developing compassion and mindfulness that allowed him to transcend his surroundings.

mediaWork.title: Ghosts Over the Boiler: Voices from Alabama's Death Row
mediaWork.creatorName: Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty (edited by Katie Owens-Murphy)
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: A collection of writings from condemned men on Alabama's death row spanning 30 years (1990-2020), providing insight into their humanity, experiences, and perspectives
mediaWork.summaryNotes:
"Ghosts Over the Boiler: Voices from Alabama's Death Row" is unique among books about wrongful convictions as it provides a platform for the voices of the men themselves, rather than focusing solely on legal analysis or journalistic accounts. The book is organized into five chronological parts spanning the 30-year history of Project Hope and includes writings that have appeared in their quarterly newsletter, "On the Wings of Hope."
Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty is particularly notable as it is a prisoner-founded and run organization established in 1989. It is run by death-sentenced inmates who solicit contributions from other death-sentenced people in Alabama, author works, and produce their quarterly newsletter.
The book deliberately avoids focusing on the crimes for which the men have been convicted, instead emphasizing their humanity, creativity, and capacity for growth and redemption. This approach challenges readers to see beyond the singular view of people on death row as defined solely by their alleged crimes.
The inclusion of Gary Drinkard's story of wrongful conviction and exoneration adds an important dimension to the book, highlighting the risk of executing innocent people. As the 93rd death row exoneree in the United States, Drinkard's experience underscores the fallibility of the criminal justice system and the irreversible nature of capital punishment.
The book serves as both a literary work and a powerful advocacy tool against the death penalty, preserving the voices and perspectives of men who have largely been silenced and forgotten by society.

mediaWork.title: He Called Me Sister: A True Story of Finding Humanity on Death Row
mediaWork.creatorName: Suzanne Craig Robertson (with foreword by Sister Helen Prejean and preface by Bill Moyers)
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: A memoir about the author's 15-year friendship with Cecil Johnson, a man on death row, and how their relationship transcended barriers of race, privilege, and circumstance
mediaWork.summaryNotes:
"He Called Me Sister: A True Story of Finding Humanity on Death Row" is not primarily focused on wrongful conviction or claims of innocence, but rather on the personal relationship that developed between the author and Cecil Johnson, a man on death row. The book offers a unique perspective on death row by focusing on the human connections that can form even in such difficult circumstances.

The story begins when the author's husband, Alan Robertson, signed up through a church program to visit Cecil Johnson on death row, offering friendship and compassion. Initially, Suzanne had no intention of being involved, but gradually, through phone calls and letters, she began to empathize with and understand Johnson. Over time, they developed a close friendship that transcended differences of race, privilege, and circumstance.

The book recounts their fifteen-year friendship and how trust and compassion were forged despite the difficult circumstances. Interestingly, the author notes that Cecil ended up ministering more to her family than they did to him, highlighting his capacity for care and compassion despite his situation.

While the book does not appear to make explicit claims about Johnson's innocence or argue that he was wrongfully convicted, it does mention that his conviction was based on eyewitness testimony without physical evidence, murder weapon, or recovered robbery proceeds. Eyewitness misidentification is known to be a leading cause of wrongful convictions, which raises questions about the reliability of the evidence in his case.

The book serves as a reminder of the humanity of people on death row and challenges readers to look beyond labels and circumstances to see the person beneath. It also implicitly raises questions about the death penalty system and its impact on all involved, including the families of those executed and the families of victims.

"Marked for Life: One Man's Fight for Justice From the Inside" is a powerful memoir by Isaac Wright Jr. with Jon Sternfeld that chronicles Wright's extraordinary journey from being wrongfully convicted as a drug kingpin to becoming a lawyer who fights for justice for others.  Published by St. Martin's Press on November 8, 2022, the 336-page hardcover book serves as the basis for the ABC television show "For Life."

mediaWork.focusOrTheme: The enormous power of American prosecutors and its contribution to mass incarceration; a new movement of reform-minded prosecutors; challenges and limitations of prosecutorial reform.

"Charged" examines the enormous power of American prosecutors in the criminal justice system and how this power has contributed to mass incarceration. Emily Bazelon, a staff writer for The New York Times Magazine and lecturer at Yale Law School, argues that over the past 40 years, prosecutors have amassed more power than the system was designed for, largely using it to put more people in prison. The book follows two main case studies: Kevin, a young man from Brooklyn who was arrested for gun possession but given a second chance through a diversion program, and Noura, who was wrongfully convicted of murdering her mother and spent 11 years incarcerated before eventually being released. Through these stories, Bazelon illustrates both the destructive potential of prosecutorial power and the promise of reform-minded approaches.

The book also documents a new movement of reform-minded prosecutors who are working to transform the system by prioritizing diversion instead of jail or prison, minimizing the use of cash bail, and addressing racial disparities. Bazelon argues that electing reform-minded district attorneys represents one of the most promising paths to reducing mass incarceration, though she acknowledges the challenges and limitations of this approach.

mediaWork.summaryNotes:
"Prosecutorial Misconduct" is a comprehensive legal treatise that establishes systematic guidelines on prosecutorial behavior, citing thousands of precedential cases. The book has become a preeminent resource for scholars and practitioners seeking guidance on wrongful convictions. It contains an extensive discussion of various types of prosecutorial misconduct and their relationship to wrongful convictions.

The book examines how prosecutors, who are constitutionally and ethically mandated to promote justice as "Ministers of Justice," sometimes deviate from these rules and engage in conduct that distorts the fact-finding process and produces erroneous convictions. Gershman argues that when prosecutors are motivated to zealously win convictions by any means and engage in conduct that either intentionally or carelessly undermines the integrity of the fact-finding process, they inevitably contribute to the conviction of innocent defendants.

The treatise covers various forms of prosecutorial misconduct, including investigative misconduct, misconduct in the grand jury, abuse of the charging function, selective and vindictive prosecution, suppression of evidence, misconduct in the plea bargaining process, misconduct in the presentation of evidence, prosecutorial-provoked mistrials, double jeopardy, misconduct at sentencing, and sanctions for misconduct.

"Gideon's Promise" is both a memoir and a call to action that explores the broken public defender system in America and presents a vision for reform. Jonathan Rapping, a MacArthur "Genius" Fellow and founder of the Gideon's Promise organization, draws from his extensive experience as a public defender and trainer to illustrate how the criminal justice system fails marginalized communities, particularly people of color and those living in poverty.

The book details Rapping's journey from his early exposure to activism through his parents to his career as a public defender and eventually founding Gideon's Promise, an organization dedicated to training and supporting public defenders across the United States. Through personal stories, case studies, and systemic analysis, Rapping argues for a "fiercely client-based ethos" in public defense and a cultural shift in how public defenders approach their work.

Rapping proposes a model for transforming the criminal justice system by building a movement of committed public defenders who can stand up against the pressures of an often callous and assembly-line approach to justice. The book emphasizes that public defenders represent over 80% of those who interact with the court system, a disproportionate number of whom are poor, non-white citizens who rely on these attorneys to navigate the law on their behalf.

mediaWork.title: Justice Failed: How "Legal Ethics" Kept Me in Prison for 26 Years
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Wrongful conviction, attorney-client privilege, legal ethics, criminal justice system failures
mediaWork.summaryNotes: This book tells the extraordinary story of Alton Logan, who was wrongfully convicted of murdering Lloyd Wickliffe at a Chicago McDonald's in 1982. The true killer, Andrew Wilson, confessed to his attorneys Dale Coventry and Jamie Kunz shortly after Logan's conviction.  Bound by attorney-client privilege, they couldn't disclose this information, instead creating a signed affidavit to be revealed after Wilson's death. Wilson died in 2007, leading to Logan's exoneration in 2008 after 26 years. The book explores the ethical dilemma faced by the attorneys and questions the balance between attorney-client privilege and justice.

mediaWork.title: Resurrected: The Innocence Portraits
mediaWork.publisherOrNetwork: Not a traditional book but an art exhibition; some paintings appear in "Illustrated Truth: Expressions of Wrongful Conviction" (2011)
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Visual representation of wrongfully convicted individuals, humanizing exonerees through portraiture
mediaWork.summaryNotes: "Resurrected: The Innocence Portraits" is not a traditional book but an art exhibition by Dan Bolick, a retired art teacher from Pittsburgh. The exhibition features large-scale portraits of 10 wrongfully convicted men who were exonerated after spending years in prison, many of them on death row. Bolick was inspired to create these portraits after his experience teaching in inner-city schools, where he saw students caught up in the criminal justice system. He wanted to raise awareness about wrongful convictions by humanizing the exonerees through his art. The exhibition was first shown at the Westmoreland Museum of American Art in Greensburg, Pennsylvania in 2009, and later at the National Underground Railroad Freedom Center in Cincinnati, Ohio in 2011. Some of Bolick's paintings were also included in the book "Illustrated Truth: Expressions of Wrongful Conviction."  What makes this project significant is its approach to raising awareness about wrongful convictions through visual art. As Bolick noted, when the issue is presented through art and the exonerees are humanized, people become more engaged and willing to discuss the problems in the criminal justice system. The portraits include the words of each subject, adding their personal narratives to the visual representation. While not a book in the traditional sense, this art series serves as an important visual resource on wrongful convictions, putting faces to the statistics and humanizing the individuals who have suffered through this injustice.

mediaWork.title: Exoneree Diaries: The Fight for Innocence, Independence, and Identity
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Life after exoneration; the challenges faced by wrongfully convicted individuals after their release
mediaWork.summaryNotes:
"Exoneree Diaries" stands out from other books on wrongful convictions by focusing not on the process of exoneration itself, but on what happens afterward. While many narratives about wrongful convictions end with the triumphant moment of release, Flowers explores the often difficult and complex journey that follows.

The book is structured around the stories of four exonerees from the Chicago area, each facing unique challenges after their release. Through these intimate portraits, Flowers reveals the psychological, social, and economic obstacles that exonerees encounter as they attempt to rebuild their lives after years or decades of wrongful imprisonment.

The book highlights how exonerees often struggle with family relationships, finding employment, adjusting to new technologies, and dealing with the psychological trauma of their experiences. Many face these challenges without the support systems and services available to guilty people released on parole.

Flowers' approach is deeply personal and humanizing, giving readers insight into the lived experiences of these individuals rather than treating them as statistics or legal case studies. The book has been praised for its thorough research and its powerful portrayal of the human cost of wrongful convictions, not just during imprisonment but in the aftermath of exoneration as well.

By focusing on Cook County, Illinois, described as "the wrongful conviction capital of the United States," the book also provides context for understanding systemic issues in the criminal justice system that contribute to wrongful convictions and the challenges faced by exonerees.

mediaWork.title: Pruno, Ramen, and a Side of Hope: Stories of Surviving Wrongful Conviction
mediaWork.creatorName: Courtney B. Lance and Nikki D. Pope
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Life during and after wrongful incarceration; how exonerees maintained hope and survived prison
mediaWork.summaryNotes: "Pruno, Ramen, and a Side of Hope" takes a unique approach to the topic of wrongful convictions by focusing on the human experience of surviving incarceration and the challenges of life after exoneration. The title refers to prison culture - "pruno" is prison-made alcohol, and ramen noodles are a staple in prison commissaries. The book weaves together personal narratives from exonerees and their families with insights into prison life, including details about prison yard gardens, contraband cooking, and family visits.  These stories reveal not just the injustice of wrongful conviction but also the resilience of the human spirit.  The book focuses on hope and survival, exploring how individuals maintained their humanity and hope in prison and addresses the challenges exonerees face after release, including employment, health, rebuilding relationships, and adjusting to societal changes.  It also includes a defense attorney's perspective and suggests ways to address systemic problems in the justice system.

mediaWork.title: Queer (In)Justice: The Criminalization of LGBT People in the United States
mediaWork.creatorName: Joey L. Mogul, Andrea J. Ritchie, and Kay Whitlock
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Examination of how the criminal justice system criminalizes, polices, and punishes LGBTQ+ people; analysis of queer criminal archetypes and their impact
mediaWork.summaryNotes: "Queer (In)Justice" provides a critical analysis of how the criminal justice system in the United States has historically and continues to criminalize LGBTQ+ people.  It examines how the entire system functions to police and punish queer identities and expressions, drawing on the authors' experience as attorneys, activists, and organizers. The book challenges mainstream LGBTQ+ rights movements, arguing for a more radical approach addressing the criminalization of LGBTQ+ people, particularly those marginalized due to race, class, and immigration status.  It reveals how criminal legal responses to LGBTQ+ people are deeply intertwined with systems of racial and economic oppression.

mediaWork.title: Worse Than Slavery: Parchman Farm And The Ordeal Of Jim Crow Justice
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: The history of Parchman Farm penitentiary in Mississippi and how the criminal justice system was used to maintain racial control after slavery
mediaWork.summaryNotes: "Worse Than Slavery" provides a comprehensive historical account of how the criminal justice system in the post-Civil War South, particularly in Mississippi, was designed to maintain racial control after the formal abolition of slavery.  The book focuses on Parchman Farm, its notorious state penitentiary, modeled after a slave plantation and synonymous with cruelty and inhumanity. Oshinsky documents how the system was weaponized against Black Americans through Black Codes and convict leasing, effectively circumventing the 13th Amendment.  While not focused on wrongful convictions, it provides context for understanding how the system was designed to control and exploit Black Americans, explaining the environment for later wrongful convictions. The book highlights the continuity between historical injustices and contemporary failures, exemplified by the cases of Levon Brooks and Kennedy Brewer.

mediaWork.title: Infinite Hope: How Wrongful Conviction, Solitary Confinement, and 12 Years on Death Row Failed to Kill My Soul
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Wrongful conviction, death penalty, solitary confinement, resilience, criminal justice reform
mediaWork.summaryNotes: "Infinite Hope" is a powerful first-person account of Anthony Graves' journey through wrongful conviction, death row, and eventual exoneration. The book not only details the legal battle for his freedom but also explores how he maintained his dignity, sanity, and hope during nearly two decades of wrongful imprisonment. After his exoneration, Graves has become a prominent advocate for criminal justice reform. He received $1.45 million in restitution for his wrongful conviction and has used his platform to raise awareness about flaws in the criminal justice system. The book serves as both a personal memoir and a call to action for systemic reform. The title "Infinite Hope" reflects Graves' enduring belief in the possibility of justice despite overwhelming odds. His story highlights both the profound failures of the criminal justice system and the resilience of the human spirit in the face of extreme adversity.

mediaWork.title: The Death of Innocents: An Eyewitness Account of Wrongful Executions
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Capital punishment, wrongful executions, criminal justice system failures, death penalty critique
mediaWork.summaryNotes: From the author of the national bestseller Dead Man Walking comes a brave and fiercely argued new book that tests the moral edge of the debate on capital punishment: What if we’re executing innocent men? Two cases in point are Dobie Gillis Williams, an indigent black man with an IQ of 65, and Joseph Roger O’Dell. Both were convicted of murder on flimsy evidence (O’Dell’s principal accuser was a jailhouse informant who later recanted his testimony). Both were executed in spite of numerous appeals. Sister Helen Prejean watched both of them die.As she recounts these men’s cases and takes us through their terrible last moments, Prejean brilliantly dismantles the legal and religious arguments that have been used to justify the death penalty. Riveting, moving, and ultimately damning, The Death of Innocents is a book we dare not ignore.
